title: EU Anti-Dumping Case on Chinese Robotic Mowers
seoTitle: EU Anti-Dumping Duties on Chinese Robotic Mowers
dek: Europe's anti-dumping investigation into robotic lawn mowers from China: what is covered, where the case stands, the duty rates reported at disclosure, and what it means for brands, factories and dealers before the 2027 season.
description: WCB's running file on EU anti-dumping case AD745 against Chinese robotic lawn mowers: timeline, scope, reported duty rates, the January 2027 deadline and analysis for Husqvarna, Positec, Mammotion and other brands.

status.label: Final decision due by 19 January 2027 · UK case opened 18 November
status.text: The European Commission sent its disclosure of essential facts on 21 October 2026, and the comment period has closed. Definitive duties, if any, must be decided by 19 January 2027. On 18 November the UK Trade Remedies Authority opened a separate investigation after a complaint from Husqvarna.

summary: On 19 November 2025 the European Commission opened anti-dumping case AD745 into robotic lawn mowers originating in China, after a complaint lodged by Husqvarna Manufacturing CZ. The product scope covers electric robotic mowers that cut grass without direct human control, with or without charging stations and navigation equipment, and both boundary-wire and wire-free models.

The case has moved slowly but steadily. Imports have been subject to registration since January 2026, which keeps open the possibility of collecting duties retroactively. In June the Commission decided not to impose provisional duties, citing the case's technical complexity. In October it issued its disclosure of essential facts, the last major step before a final decision.

Europe is the most developed robotic mower market and the main battleground for Chinese brands that have grown on wire-free navigation, RTK, vision and all-wheel drive. A definitive duty would raise the cost of China-made mowers just as dealers place orders for the 2027 spring season, and would reward companies that have already moved production elsewhere.

callout.title: Reported duty rates at disclosure (unconfirmed)
callout.text: Trade publications citing the Commission's 21 October document report proposed rates of 45.6% for Mammotion, 53.3% for Positec, 47.0% for other cooperating producers and 53.3% for everyone else, charged on the CIF price at the EU border. The disclosure is confidential, the Commission has not published these figures, and final rates can change after parties comment.

questions.q: Are EU anti-dumping duties already being charged on Chinese robotic mowers?
questions.a: Not yet. No provisional duty was imposed, and as of 19 November 2026 no definitive measure had been published. Imports were registered from January 2026, but press accounts of the October disclosure say the Commission is not proposing to collect duties retroactively.

Electric robotic lawn mowers originating in China that cut grass without direct human control, whether they use boundary wires or wire-free navigation, and whether they are sold alone or with charging stations and navigation equipment.

questions.q: How high could the duties be?
questions.a: The Commission has not published rates. Press accounts of the October disclosure report 45.6% for Mammotion, 53.3% for Positec, 47.0% for other cooperating producers and 53.3% for the rest, charged on the CIF border price. Those figures are unconfirmed and can change before the final regulation.

questions.q: Does production outside China avoid the duties?
questions.a: Anti-dumping duties apply by country of origin, so mowers genuinely produced outside China are not covered. Simply routing Chinese products through another country can be treated as circumvention, and the EU can extend duties to such flows.

questions.q: How does this connect to the US FCC restrictions?
questions.a: They are separate measures. The EU case concerns pricing and origin, and only covers China. The US FCC Covered List concerns national security and covers robotic mowers produced anywhere outside the US. Together they squeeze China-made mowers in both of the category's largest markets at once.

questions.q: Why are the reported rates close to 50%?
questions.a: Because the Commission found significant distortions in China's economy, it did not use Chinese costs to set a fair price. It built a normal value from costs in a representative country, reported to be Malaysia, and compared that with export prices to the EU. That method usually produces higher margins than a comparison with Chinese domestic prices.

questions.q: Will duties be charged on mowers imported in 2026?
questions.a: Registration from 24 January 2026 made that legally possible, but press accounts of the disclosure say the Commission is not proposing retroactive collection. If that holds, duties start from the day after the definitive regulation is published.

questions.q: Does the EU decision apply in the UK?
questions.a: No. The UK runs its own trade remedies system. The Trade Remedies Authority opened a separate investigation into Chinese robot lawn mowers on 18 November 2026 after a complaint from Husqvarna, with its own timetable and an extra economic interest test.

questions.q: How much would a 47% duty add to a mower?
questions.a: The duty is charged on the customs value at the border, not the shop price. A mower entering the EU at €500 CIF would carry about €235 of anti-dumping duty at 47%, before regular customs duty and VAT.

sections.title: Where the EU and UK cases stand
sections.intro: The EU case is one vote away from a decision. The UK case has just started and will run through most of 2027.

sections.title: What to watch next
sections.intro: The investigation is in its final stretch. These are the steps between the disclosure and duties at the border, and the dates that matter for 2027 orders.

cells: Producers, importers and Husqvarna answered the Commission's findings. Rates can still move, usually down for companies that win corrections.
Companies that want a say in the UK case must register with the Trade Remedies Authority.
The Commission puts its draft regulation to the member-state trade defence committee before adopting it.
If adopted, duties apply from the day after publication in the Official Journal, normally for five years.
Dealer orders and retail prices for the 2027 season will show who absorbed the duty and who moved production.
Companies can challenge the regulation at the EU General Court. Shipments routed through other countries can be targeted by an anti-circumvention case.

sections.title: Why the proposed rates are so high
sections.intro: The Commission found 'significant distortions' in China's economy, so it did not use Chinese prices and costs to work out a fair price. It built a normal value from costs in a representative third country, reported to be Malaysia, and compared that with export prices to the EU. Chinese exporters argue their EU prices are above their prices at home, but under these rules the test is the constructed value, not the Chinese domestic price. Sampled companies get their own rate; cooperating companies outside the sample get an average, and the residual rate for everyone else is usually set at the highest level found.

sections.title: What the duty adds per mower
sections.intro: Anti-dumping duty is charged on the customs value at the EU border (CIF), before regular customs duty and VAT. These examples show the extra cost per unit at the reported rates. They are illustrations, not quotes.

table.note: Rounded to the nearest euro. VAT is then charged on the duty-inclusive value, so the retail effect is larger than the duty alone.

charts.title: Border value of one mower, before and after the duty
charts.note: Illustrations at the reported rates, before regular customs duty and VAT. VAT is then charged on the higher value, so the shelf price rises by more.

sections.title: Who is on each side
sections.intro: Duties follow where a mower is made, not where the brand is based. Click a company for its profile. Production sites are those the companies name themselves; a single model can come from elsewhere, so check its label and declaration before ordering.

cells: Its Czech unit filed the EU complaint and its UK business in Newton Aycliffe filed the UK one. Gains price protection in both markets if duties follow.
Lowest reported company rate. Sells LUBA and YUKA models across Europe.
Kress says much of its range is now made outside China; its Voyager and MasterSeries models are still China-made, Motorist reported.
Ninebot told investors in June 2026 it has partly built a 'China plus overseas' supply chain and that the case could affect its business.
Cooperating companies outside the sample get 47.0%, others 53.3%. Which brands cooperated has not been published.
